learn.hook: What if a river could talk to you? What advice would it give?
points: The lesson 'The Day the River Spoke' is about a girl, a river and her wish to learn. Here we read our own short story on the same idea.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when) and a plot (what happens).
The theme is the big idea or message of a story, such as courage or the right to learn.
Personification gives human actions to non-living things: 'The river whispered a secret.'
Clues in the text help us infer feelings: a girl who whispers her wish may feel shy or unsure.

example.q: Read: Every morning, Meera sat on the steps by the river and watched children walk to school with their bags. "I want to read books too," she whispered. The river splashed softly and said, "Go on, little one. Even I keep moving forward." The next day, Meera asked her father if she could join the village school. How does Meera feel at first, and what helps her act?
steps: Find the clue: she 'whispered' her wish, so she feels shy but longs to study.
Notice what changes: the river tells her to keep moving forward.
See the result: the next day she asks her father about school.
example.answer: At first Meera longs to study but is shy; the river's words give her courage, so she asks her father to let her join school.

learn.reallife: When you look at a river, a tree or the moon and imagine it talking, you are using personification, just like poets and storytellers do.

games.title: Story sequence
items: Meera watches children walk to school.
She whispers her wish to read books.
The river tells her to keep moving forward.
Meera asks her father if she can join school.

games.title: Story elements
items: The setting tells where and when a story happens.
Setting = place and time of the story.
Personification compares two things using 'like' or 'as'.
That is a simile. Personification gives human qualities to things.
The plot is the chain of events in a story.
Plot is what happens, from beginning to end.
'The wind whistled a happy tune' is an example of personification.
Wind cannot really whistle a tune; it is given a human action.
The theme of a story is the same thing as its title.
The title is the name; the theme is the big idea or message.

quiz.q: 'Every morning, Meera sat on the steps by the river and watched children walk to school.' What is the setting of this line?
options: The steps by a river, in the morning
A busy market in the evening
quiz.explain: The line says Meera sat 'on the steps by the river' 'every morning' — that is the place and time.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the place the other children are going to with the place where Meera is

quiz.q: '"I want to read books too," Meera whispered.' What does Meera wish for?
options: To buy a new school bag
To study and read like the other children
To stay at home all day
quiz.explain: She says she wants to read books 'too', like the children going to school.
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail (the bags) instead of what she actually says

quiz.q: 'The river splashed softly and said, "Go on, little one."' Which figure of speech is used here?
quiz.explain: A river cannot speak, so giving it speech is personification.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any imaginative line is a simile, even without 'like' or 'as'

quiz.q: Which sentence uses personification?
options: The river sang a soft song to the girl.
The river was cold and clear.
The river is near the village.
quiz.explain: Only a person can sing a song; giving this action to a river is personification.
quiz.mistake: Thinks describing a thing with adjectives is personification

quiz.q: 'Meera whispered her wish so that no one could hear.' This most likely shows that she feels:
quiz.explain: Whispering so no one hears suggests she is shy or not sure anyone will listen.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the clue word 'whispered' to infer the feeling

quiz.q: What is the theme of a story?
options: The number of pages in it
The name of the main character
The place where it was printed
The big idea or message the story shares
quiz.explain: The theme is the central idea, like 'every child deserves to learn'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up theme with other facts about a book

quiz.q: '"Even I keep moving forward," said the river.' What lesson does the river give Meera?
options: Keep going and don't stop trying
quiz.explain: A river always flows on; it tells Meera to keep moving towards her goal.
quiz.mistake: Reads the line literally instead of as advice

quiz.q: 'The next day, Meera asked her father if she could join the village school.' This shows that Meera:
options: found the courage to act on her wish
quiz.explain: She moves from only wishing to actually asking — that takes courage.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the ending with how the character has changed

teach.ask: Tweet! Gappu saw a story where a river talks! Can rivers really talk? What do we call it when a writer makes a river act like a person?
teach.praise: Wow! So when I say 'the sun smiled', I'm using personification too!
teach.nudge: But what kind of things get human actions in personification?

learn.hook: In 1848, Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule started a school for girls in Pune, when very few girls in India went to school.
points: Education means learning and growing by reading, thinking and asking questions.
When girls study, they can follow their dreams, earn a living and help their families and villages.
India's Right to Education Act (2009) gives every child aged 6 to 14 the right to free and compulsory schooling.
Word family: educate (verb), education (noun), educated (adjective), educator (a person who teaches).
Literate means able to read and write; its opposite is illiterate.

example.q: Read: Ritu's grandmother never went to school. Now Ritu teaches her the letters on bus boards, and Nani proudly reads out the name of their town. What does this show?
steps: Ritu learned at school.
She shares her learning with her grandmother.
Nani learns to read even when she is old.
example.answer: Learning can happen at any age, and an educated girl can spread her learning to her whole family.

learn.reallife: Look around: girls and women work as doctors, pilots, scientists, teachers and police officers — education opened those doors.

games.title: Words about learning
pairs: a strong wish to achieve something
money given to help a student study

quiz.q: Which word means 'able to read and write'?
quiz.explain: Literate means able to read and write. Literature means books and writing; literal means exact.
quiz.mistake: Confuses words that look alike

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'literate'?
quiz.explain: The prefix il- is used before words starting with l: literate → illiterate.
quiz.mistake: Uses the common prefix un- or dis- without checking the correct form

quiz.q: India's Right to Education Act gives free and compulsory schooling to children aged:
quiz.explain: The Right to Education Act, 2009 covers children from 6 to 14 years of age.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a familiar school-age range instead of the one in the law

quiz.q: Who, along with Jyotirao Phule, started a school for girls in Pune in 1848?
quiz.explain: Savitribai Phule taught at the girls' school she and Jyotirao Phule started in Pune in 1848.
quiz.mistake: Picks another famous Indian woman without matching her work

quiz.q: Which word in this family is a noun: educate, education, educated, educational?
quiz.explain: 'Education' names a thing (the process of learning). 'Educate' is a verb; 'educated' and 'educational' are adjectives.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice how endings like -ion, -ed and -al change the word class

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'My aunt is an ___ woman; she has a college degree.'
quiz.explain: An adjective is needed to describe 'woman', so 'educated' fits.
quiz.mistake: Uses the verb or noun form where an adjective is needed

quiz.q: 'Ritu teaches her grandmother to read the names on bus boards.' What does this tell us?
options: People can learn at any age
Bus boards are hard to find
Ritu does not go to school
quiz.explain: Nani is learning to read in her old age, so learning has no age limit.
quiz.mistake: Adds an idea that is not in the text

quiz.q: Which sentence BEST matches the idea of 'education for all'?
options: School is only for children in cities.
Only boys need to go to school.
Every child, girl or boy, should get the chance to learn.
quiz.explain: 'For all' means everyone — every girl and every boy, in villages and cities.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand that 'all' includes everyone

teach.ask: Gappu asks: why should girls go to school just like boys?
teach.praise: Yes! Every chick in the nest deserves to learn to fly — girls and boys!
teach.nudge: Can you tell me what education helps girls do in their future?

learn.hook: The words river, Narmada, flock and hope are all nouns — but each is a different kind!
points: A noun is a naming word for a person, place, animal, thing or idea.
Common noun: a general name — girl, river, school.
Proper noun: a special name that begins with a capital letter — Meera, Narmada, Pune, Diwali.
Collective noun: a name for a group — a flock of birds, a herd of cows, a bunch of keys.
Abstract noun: a quality, feeling or idea you cannot touch — courage, honesty, knowledge, friendship.

example.q: Find the nouns and their kinds: 'A class of girls showed great courage on the banks of the Ganga.'
steps: 'class' names a group → collective noun
'girls' and 'banks' are general names → common nouns
'courage' is a quality we cannot touch → abstract noun
'Ganga' is a special name with a capital letter → proper noun
example.answer: class (collective), girls and banks (common), courage (abstract), Ganga (proper)

learn.reallife: Shop signs, maps and your school ID card are full of proper nouns — that's why they begin with capital letters.

items.text: a ___ of grapes
a ___ of bees
a ___ of cows
a ___ of birds
a ___ of lions

quiz.q: Which of these is a proper noun?
quiz.explain: Kaveri is the special name of one river, so it is a proper noun and starts with a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any place word is a proper noun

quiz.q: Which of these is an abstract noun?
quiz.explain: Honesty is a quality — you cannot see or touch it. The others are things or people.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that abstract nouns name qualities and feelings

quiz.q: 'A herd of elephants crossed the river.' Which word is the collective noun?
quiz.explain: 'Herd' is the name for a group of elephants.
quiz.mistake: Picks the animals instead of the word naming their group

quiz.q: Complete: 'a ___ of fish'
quiz.explain: A group of fish swimming together is called a school (or shoal).
quiz.mistake: Uses a group word that belongs to other animals

quiz.q: Which words need capital letters in: 'meera visited jaipur in december.'?
quiz.explain: The first word of a sentence and proper nouns (a name, a city, a month) begin with capital letters.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that names of places and months are proper nouns

quiz.q: 'Her kindness made everyone smile.' The word 'kindness' is:
quiz.explain: Kindness is a quality we feel but cannot touch, so it is an abstract noun.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only things you can touch can be nouns

quiz.q: What is the noun form of 'brave'?
quiz.explain: 'Bravery' names the quality. 'Bravely' is an adverb; 'braver' and 'bravest' are adjectives.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the noun with other forms of the word

quiz.q: Complete: 'a ___ of wolves'
quiz.explain: A group of wolves is called a pack.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up collective nouns for different animals

teach.ask: Gappu found the words 'Meera', 'river' and 'courage'. Are they all the same kind of noun? Explain to him.
teach.praise: Chirp! Meera is proper, river is common and courage is abstract. Got it!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what kind of noun is 'courage' — something you can touch?

learn.hook: Did you know that most good things — riding a cycle, swimming, writing neatly — took many tries before they worked?
points: The poem 'Try Again' encourages us to keep trying after we fail. Here is our own poem on the same idea.
A poem is written in lines; a group of lines is called a stanza.
Rhyming words end with the same sound: two/do, tail/fail, say/way.
The rhyme scheme uses letters: lines that rhyme get the same letter, e.g. aabb.
Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult.

example.q: Read: My kite fell down, it tore in two, / I sighed, "Now what am I to do?" / I tied the string, I fixed the tail, / I tried again — this time, no fail! / If once you slip, then rise and say, / "I'll try again, a better way." What is the rhyme scheme, and what is the message?
steps: two/do rhyme → a a
tail/fail rhyme → b b
say/way rhyme → c c
The child fixes the kite and tries again instead of giving up.
example.answer: The rhyme scheme is aabbcc; the message is: when you fail, rise and try again in a better way.

learn.reallife: Sports stars, scientists and even your favourite cricketers failed many times before they succeeded. They persevered.

games.title: Never give up
items: Ravi wobbled and fell off his new bicycle.
He brushed off the dust and got back on.
He practised every evening in the lane.
At last, he rode all the way to the park and back.

quiz.q: 'My kite fell down, it tore in two, / I sighed, "Now what am I to do?"' Which word rhymes with 'two'?
quiz.explain: 'Two' and 'do' end with the same 'oo' sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that only starts with the same letter

quiz.q: The lines of a poem end with: two, do, tail, fail. What is the rhyme scheme?
quiz.explain: two/do rhyme (a a), tail/fail rhyme (b b), so the scheme is aabb.
quiz.mistake: Does not give the same letter to lines that rhyme

quiz.q: What does 'perseverance' mean?
options: continuing to try in spite of difficulty
quiz.explain: Perseverance is not stopping when things are hard.
quiz.mistake: Confuses perseverance with luck or easy success

quiz.q: 'I tied the string, I fixed the tail, / I tried again — this time, no fail!' What did the child do after the kite tore?
quiz.explain: The child tied the string, fixed the tail and tried again.
quiz.mistake: Guesses instead of reading the lines

quiz.q: 'If once you slip, then rise and say...' In this poem, 'slip' most nearly means:
quiz.explain: Here 'slip' is used to mean failing once, and 'rise' means trying again.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word only in its literal sense

quiz.q: A group of lines in a poem is called a:
quiz.explain: Poems are divided into stanzas; stories into paragraphs and chapters; plays into scenes.
quiz.mistake: Uses the word for parts of a story or play

quiz.q: A line or phrase that is repeated again and again in a poem is called a:
quiz.explain: A refrain is a repeated line, like 'try again' in many poems on perseverance.
quiz.mistake: Confuses repetition with the title or rhyme pattern

quiz.q: Which proverb matches the message of the poem?
options: An apple a day keeps the doctor away.
If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
quiz.explain: The poem is about not giving up after failing — exactly what this proverb says.
quiz.mistake: Picks a familiar proverb without matching its meaning

teach.ask: Gappu fell while learning to fly and wants to quit. What does 'perseverance' mean? Tell him!
teach.praise: Okay, okay! I'll flap again tomorrow, and the day after, until I fly!
teach.nudge: But what should I do when it gets hard — stop or keep going?

topics.title: Never give up: words of courage

learn.hook: 'Give up', 'carry on', 'keep on' — tiny words like 'up' and 'on' completely change the meaning of a verb!
points: 'Give up' is a phrasal verb meaning 'stop trying'; 'carry on' and 'keep on' mean 'continue'.
Synonyms have similar meanings: determined, resolute, firm.
Antonyms are opposites; many are made with prefixes: un-, dis-, im-, in-, ir-, il-.
We often use im- before b, m, p (impossible, impatient), ir- before r (irregular) and il- before l (illegal).
Persistent means continuing firmly, never stopping trying.

example.q: Change these words to their opposites: possible, patient, regular, legal.
steps: possible starts with p → impossible
patient starts with p → impatient
regular starts with r → irregular
legal starts with l → illegal
example.answer: impossible, impatient, irregular, illegal

learn.reallife: Coaches, teachers and parents say 'Don't give up!' and 'Keep it up!' — now you know these are phrasal verbs.

items.text: Don't ___ now; the finish line is just ahead!
Keep ___ trying, and you will get better.
Sana was ___ to win the race, so she trained every day.
The puzzle was hard, but Kabir was ___ and solved it in the end.

quiz.q: 'Don't give up!' means:
quiz.explain: The phrasal verb 'give up' means to stop trying or quit.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'give up' word by word instead of as one phrasal verb

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'determined'?
quiz.explain: Resolute means firm in purpose — the same as determined.
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'patient'?
quiz.explain: Words starting with p often take im-: impatient, impossible, impolite.
quiz.mistake: Uses a common prefix without knowing the correct one

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'regular'?
quiz.explain: Before r, the prefix becomes ir-: irregular, irresponsible.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the ir- prefix

quiz.q: 'Even after losing twice, Arjun did not quit. He decided to ___ practising.'
quiz.explain: He did not quit, so he decided to continue — 'carry on'.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the clue 'did not quit'

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'success'?
quiz.explain: Success means achieving your aim; failure means not achieving it.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word connected to success instead of its opposite

quiz.q: Which word means 'continuing firmly and not stopping trying'?
quiz.explain: A persistent person keeps on trying.
quiz.mistake: Confuses persistent with words that mean unsure or careless

quiz.q: What does 'Practice makes perfect' mean?
options: Doing something again and again makes you better at it.
Practice is a waste of time.
You must be perfect before you practise.
quiz.explain: Repeating and practising a skill is how we improve.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the cause and the result

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know: what are some ways to say 'keep trying', and what is the opposite?
teach.praise: Super! I will carry on and be persistent — no giving up for Gappu!
teach.nudge: And what phrasal verb means the opposite — to quit?

learn.hook: Helen Keller could not see or hear — yet she wrote books, travelled the world and earned a college degree!
points: Helen Keller (1880–1968) was an American writer. An illness took away her sight and hearing when she was about 19 months old.

Her teacher Anne Sullivan taught her words by spelling them into her hand. Her big breakthrough came when she understood that the letters spelled into her palm meant the 'water' pouring over her other hand.
In 1904 she graduated from Radcliffe College — the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree.
'Three Days to See' is an essay in which she imagines what she would look at if she could see for three days.
An essay is a short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's thoughts and feelings.

example.q: Read this short piece in the spirit of the essay: "If I could see for just one day, I would first look at my mother's face. Then I would gaze at a marigold garland, bright orange and gold. At night I would lie on the roof and count the stars until I fell asleep." What is the writer asking us to value?
steps: List what the writer wants to see: a loved face, colours, the stars.
These are everyday sights we often ignore.
So the message is to notice and treasure what we can see.
example.answer: To treasure the ordinary sights around us — faces, colours and the night sky — instead of taking them for granted.

learn.reallife: Next time you see a sunset or your friend's smile, pause for a moment and really look — that is what Helen Keller asked people to do.

quiz.q: 'Three Days to See' by Helen Keller is:

quiz.q: What is an essay?

A story acted on a stage
A short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's ideas
quiz.explain: Essays are in prose (not verse) and share a writer's thoughts on one topic.

quiz.q: What is the main message of 'Three Days to See'?

We should use our senses fully and not take them for granted
quiz.explain: Helen Keller urges sighted people to look closely at the world as if they might lose their sight tomorrow.

quiz.q: Helen Keller was the first deafblind person to earn:
quiz.explain: She graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904 with a BA degree.

quiz.q: 'If I could see for just one day, I would first look at my mother's face.' What would the writer look at first?
quiz.explain: The word 'first' tells us the mother's face comes before the garland and the stars.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the order word 'first'

quiz.q: To 'take something for granted' means to:
options: not value it because you always have it
give it away as a gift
quiz.explain: When we take sight for granted, we forget how precious it is.

teach.ask: Gappu heard about 'Three Days to See'. Who wrote it, and what is it about?
teach.praise: Wow! I'll look at the sky with fresh eyes today!
teach.nudge: And what does she want us to do with our senses?

learn.hook: Your nose can recognise the smell of hot jalebis even before you see the shop!
points: We have five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue) and touch (skin).
Sensory words help readers imagine: glittering (sight), crackling (sound), fragrant (smell), tangy (taste), velvety (touch).
Braille is a reading system of raised dots invented by Louis Braille of France. Each Braille cell has six dot positions.
People who are deaf may use sign language; India has its own Indian Sign Language (ISL).
Melodious means sweet-sounding; fragrant means sweet-smelling.

example.q: Which senses are used in: 'The sizzling jalebis smelled sweet and felt sticky in my fingers'?
steps: 'sizzling' is a sound → hearing
'smelled sweet' → smell
'felt sticky' → touch
example.answer: Hearing, smell and touch

learn.reallife: Lifts, ATMs and some medicine boxes have Braille dots so that people who cannot see can use them.

quiz.q: Which word appeals to our sense of hearing?
quiz.explain: Rustling is the sound of dry leaves or paper moving.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sound words with smell, touch or sight words

quiz.q: 'The mogra flowers were fragrant.' Which sense does 'fragrant' appeal to?
quiz.explain: Fragrant means having a sweet smell.
quiz.mistake: Thinks of how flowers look instead of the meaning of 'fragrant'

quiz.q: Who invented the Braille system of reading?
quiz.explain: Louis Braille of France created the raised-dot system that is named after him.
quiz.mistake: Picks another famous inventor

quiz.q: How many dot positions are there in one Braille cell?
quiz.explain: A Braille cell has 6 dot positions in two columns of three; different patterns stand for different letters.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without knowing the 2-by-3 pattern

quiz.q: Which word appeals to our sense of touch?
quiz.explain: Rough describes how something feels to our skin.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up touch with other senses

quiz.q: Which sense organ helps us taste food?
quiz.explain: Taste buds on the tongue tell sweet, sour, salty and bitter.
quiz.mistake: Confuses taste with smell, which also helps with flavour

quiz.q: What does 'melodious' mean?
quiz.explain: Melodious comes from 'melody' — a tune — so it means pleasant to hear.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the word to its root 'melody'

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the sense of taste?
quiz.explain: Sour is a taste.
quiz.mistake: Does not match the describing word to its sense

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why Helen Keller said we should treasure our senses. What are our senses and why should we value them?
teach.praise: Tweet! I can see, hear, smell, taste and touch — I'm so lucky!
teach.nudge: Name the senses, and tell me why they are precious.

learn.hook: Good, better, best! Some adjectives change completely when we compare.
points: Positive degree describes one thing: tall, beautiful.
Comparative degree compares two things and is often followed by 'than': taller, more beautiful.
Superlative degree compares three or more and usually takes 'the': the tallest, the most beautiful.
Long adjectives use more/most: more precious, most precious.
Irregular forms: good–better–best, bad–worse–worst, many–more–most, little–less–least. Spelling: big–bigger, happy–happier.

example.q: Complete: 'The Taj Mahal looks ___ (beautiful) at sunrise than at noon.'
steps: Two times are compared (sunrise and noon), and 'than' follows → comparative.
'Beautiful' is a long word, so we use 'more'.
example.answer: more beautiful

learn.reallife: Shops say 'Bigger! Better! Best!' and sports reporters say 'the fastest bowler' — that's degrees of comparison.

items.text: Rohan is ___ than his brother.
This is the ___ day of my life!
My cold is ___ today than yesterday.
Of all the senses, sight seemed the ___ precious to her.

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'good'?
quiz.explain: 'Good' is irregular: good – better – best.
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to an irregular adjective

quiz.q: What is the superlative degree of 'bad'?
quiz.explain: 'Bad' is irregular: bad – worse – worst.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the comparative 'worse' with the superlative 'worst'

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Mount Everest is the most high mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is highest than all mountains.
Mount Everest is the higher mountain in the world.
quiz.explain: Comparing with all mountains needs the superlative with 'the': the highest.
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative when comparing more than two

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: When an adjective ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happier.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the y → i spelling rule or uses 'more' with -er

quiz.q: 'Of all my senses, I think sight is the ___ precious.'
quiz.explain: 'Of all' compares many, so we need the superlative 'most'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative when comparing more than two

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'big'?
quiz.explain: Short words ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: big → bigger.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the final consonant

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the positive degree?
options: Ravi is the tallest in class.
quiz.explain: 'Tall' describes Ravi without comparing — positive degree.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with an adjective is comparative

quiz.q: 'In May, Delhi is ___ than Shimla.'
quiz.explain: Two places are compared with 'than', so the comparative 'hotter' is needed.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the word 'than'

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'This mango is gooder than that one, and it is the most best!' Help him with degrees of comparison.
teach.praise: Ah! This mango is better, and that one is the best! Yum!
teach.nudge: What are the correct words instead of 'gooder' and 'most best'?

learn.hook: Imagine asking a cat why it knocks things off the table — and getting an answer!
points: Doctor Dolittle is a character created by the English writer Hugh Lofting. He is a doctor who learns to talk with animals.
In the stories, his parrot Polynesia teaches him the language of animals, and he becomes a doctor for animals.
A doctor who treats animals is called a veterinarian, or vet.
Real animals communicate with sounds, movements and smells — honeybees even do a 'waggle dance' to show where flowers are.
Our own story below imagines a clinic where a bird helps a doctor understand animals.

example.q: Read: Dr Mehta's clinic in Pune was full of patients — but none of them were people! A goat with a sore hoof bleated, "Ma-a-a, my foot hurts!" Mynah, the clinic's chatty bird, flapped her wings and explained the problem to the doctor. "Thank you, Mynah," smiled Dr Mehta. "What would I do without my translator?" Why does Dr Mehta call Mynah his 'translator'?
steps: A translator changes words from one language into another.
The goat speaks in animal language; Mynah explains it to the doctor.
So Mynah does a translator's job.
example.answer: Because Mynah turns the animals' language into words the doctor can understand.

learn.reallife: Vets at animal hospitals and gaushalas read animals' body language — a limping goat or a cat that won't eat tells them something is wrong.

games.title: Dolittle and doctors
items: Doctor Dolittle was created by Hugh Lofting.
Hugh Lofting, an English writer, created him.
In the stories, Doctor Dolittle learns animal language from his parrot.
A vet is a doctor who treats animals.
Doctor Dolittle is a real doctor who lived in Pune.
He is an imaginary character in English storybooks.
Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
This is called the waggle dance.

quiz.q: Who created the character Doctor Dolittle?
quiz.explain: Hugh Lofting, an English writer, wrote the Doctor Dolittle books.

quiz.q: A doctor who treats animals is called a:
quiz.explain: Veterinarians (vets) treat animals. A paediatrician treats children; an optician deals with eyes and glasses.
quiz.mistake: Confuses different kinds of doctors

quiz.explain: Goats and sheep bleat. Horses neigh, elephants trumpet and owls hoot.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up animal sounds

quiz.q: 'Mynah flapped her wings and explained the problem to the doctor. "What would I do without my translator?" said Dr Mehta.' Why is Mynah called a translator?

She sings songs for the patients
quiz.explain: A translator changes one language into another; Mynah turns animal talk into human words.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'translator'

quiz.q: What does 'translate' mean?

quiz.explain: To translate is to put words into a different language.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the sound of the word

quiz.q: Which of these is a REAL way animals communicate?
options: A cat reads the morning newspaper.
A cow writes a letter to the farmer.
Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
A goat speaks Hindi to the vet.
quiz.explain: The honeybee's waggle dance is a real way of sharing information. The others are fantasy.
quiz.mistake: Cannot tell real animal behaviour from fantasy

options: The doctor was not at work
We expect patients to be humans, but they are animals
quiz.explain: The surprise twist — the patients are animals — makes us smile.
quiz.mistake: Misses the surprise in the second half of the sentence

teach.ask: Gappu wants a doctor who understands chirps! Who is Doctor Dolittle and what is special about him?
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Doctor Dolittle would understand me perfectly!
teach.nudge: What is special about the way he talks to his patients?

learn.hook: A crocodile booking a train ticket to visit the dentist? That's imagination at work!
points: Fantasy describes things that cannot happen in real life, like talking animals or flying carpets.
Realistic writing describes things that could really happen.
Humour comes from surprise, silly situations, funny talk and exaggeration.
Exaggeration (hyperbole) makes something sound much bigger than it is: 'I've told you a million times!'
Word family: imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginary and imaginative (adjectives).

example.q: Is this fantasy or real, and why is it funny? 'The crocodile booked a train ticket to Chennai to see the dentist.'
steps: Crocodiles cannot book tickets → fantasy.
A huge-toothed crocodile worried about its teeth is a silly surprise.
example.answer: It is fantasy, and it is funny because of the silly, surprising situation.

learn.reallife: Cartoons, comics and funny ads on TV use talking animals and exaggeration to make us laugh.

games.title: Fantasy or real?
items: A tortoise flies a kite over Jaipur.
A camel reads the morning newspaper.
A crow becomes the class monitor.
An elephant plays the tabla at a wedding.

quiz.q: Which sentence is fantasy?
options: A tiger opens a sweet shop in Kolkata.
A tiger rests in the shade.
quiz.explain: Tigers cannot run shops, so that sentence is fantasy.
quiz.mistake: Does not separate imagined events from real ones

quiz.q: Which sentence is realistic?
options: A dog teaches maths to puppies.
A dog barks at the postman.
A dog writes a poem about the moon.
A dog drives a bus to school.
quiz.explain: Dogs really do bark at strangers; the others cannot happen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything with an animal is fantasy

quiz.q: 'This bag weighs a ton!' is an example of:
quiz.explain: A school bag doesn't really weigh a ton; the speaker is exaggerating for effect.
quiz.mistake: Takes the exaggeration as a comparison

quiz.q: Why do writers add humour to stories?
options: To entertain readers and make them smile
quiz.explain: Humour makes reading fun and keeps us interested.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the writer's purpose

quiz.q: What does 'imaginary' mean?
quiz.explain: Something imaginary is made up, not real.
quiz.mistake: Confuses imaginary with real

quiz.q: Which word in this family is a noun: imagine, imagination, imaginary, imaginative?
quiz.explain: 'Imagination' names the ability; 'imagine' is a verb and the other two are adjectives.
quiz.mistake: Does not use word endings to find the word class

quiz.q: Which sentence uses exaggeration?
options: I'm so hungry I could eat a whole elephant!
quiz.explain: Nobody can eat an elephant — the speaker exaggerates to show great hunger.
quiz.mistake: Picks a plain fact

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'serious'?
quiz.explain: Grave, solemn and stern all mean serious; funny is the opposite.
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

teach.ask: Gappu laughed at a story about a goat visiting the doctor. What makes such a story fantasy, and why is it funny?
teach.praise: Hee hee! Animals talking is fantasy, and the silly surprises make me giggle!
teach.nudge: Could it really happen? And what makes us laugh?

learn.hook: Quotation marks are like a speech bubble in a comic — they hold a speaker's exact words.
points: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: Mynah said, "The goat is hurt."
The spoken words begin with a capital letter, and a comma, full stop, question mark or exclamation mark comes before the closing quotation mark.
Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quotation marks, often using 'that': Mynah said that the goat was hurt.
When the reporting verb is in the past (said), the tense usually moves back: am/is → was, can → could, will → would, like → liked.
Pronouns change to fit: Rohan said, "I am tired." → Rohan said that he was tired. Universal truths stay in the present tense.

example.q: Change to reported speech: Rohan said, "I can help the goat."
steps: Remove the quotation marks and add 'that'.
'I' (Rohan) becomes 'he'.
'can' moves back to 'could' because 'said' is past.
example.answer: Rohan said that he could help the goat.

learn.reallife: News reports, comics and your diary use both — direct speech for exact words, reported speech to retell them.

items.text: He said, "I am sleepy." → He said that he ___ sleepy.
She said, "I can run fast." → She said that she ___ run fast.
They said, "We will come." → They said that they ___ come.
Raju said, "I like dogs." → Raju said that he ___ dogs.

games.title: Build the sentence
games.prompt: Arrange to make correct direct speech

quiz.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Priya said, The parrot can talk.
quiz.explain: A comma after 'said', quotation marks around the exact words, a capital T, and the full stop inside the closing marks.
quiz.mistake: Puts quotation marks around the wrong words or forgets the capital letter

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: Arun said, "I am hungry."
options: Arun says that I was hungry.
Arun said that he were hungry.
Arun said that he was hungry.
Arun said that I am hungry.
quiz.explain: 'I' becomes 'he' and 'am' moves back to 'was'.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the pronoun or the tense

quiz.q: In reported speech after 'said', 'will' usually changes to:
quiz.explain: The past form of 'will' is 'would'.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the past form of the modal

quiz.q: Which sentence is in direct speech?
options: Meena said that she loved mangoes.
quiz.explain: Direct speech shows the exact words inside quotation marks.
quiz.mistake: Confuses reported speech with direct speech

quiz.q: What do quotation marks show?
options: the title of a chapter only
quiz.explain: Quotation marks (inverted commas) go around a speaker's exact words.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the main use of quotation marks

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: Sita said, "I can swim."
options: Sita said that she could swam.
Sita said that she can swims.
Sita said that she could swim.
Sita said that I could swim.
quiz.explain: 'I' becomes 'she', and 'can' becomes 'could' followed by the base verb 'swim'.
quiz.mistake: Changes the main verb instead of the modal

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: The teacher said, "The Earth goes around the Sun."
options: The teacher said that the Earth is going around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth went around the Sun yesterday.
The teacher said that the Earth goes around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth had gone around the Sun.
quiz.explain: A universal truth stays in the simple present even in reported speech.
quiz.mistake: Changes the tense of a universal truth

quiz.q: Ravi asked, "Can animals talk" — where should the question mark go?
quiz.explain: The question mark belongs to the spoken question, so it goes inside: Ravi asked, "Can animals talk?"
quiz.mistake: Places the question mark outside the quotation marks

teach.ask: Gappu wrote: Mynah said I am hungry. What is missing in direct speech, and how do we report it?
teach.praise: So it's: Mynah said, "I am hungry." Or: Mynah said that she was hungry. Neat!
teach.nudge: Where do the quotation marks and comma go? And how would we report it with 'that'?

learn.hook: Some poems are written just to make you giggle — and that's a serious skill!
points: 'A Funny Man' is a humorous poem about a person who does odd, funny things. Here is our own funny poem.
A humorous poem makes us laugh with silly people, odd actions and surprising rhymes.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem — the pattern of strong and weak sounds you can clap to.
Two lines next to each other that rhyme are called a rhyming couplet (rhyme scheme aabb).
Sound words like 'click-clack' are called onomatopoeia.

example.q: Read: Uncle Bholu wore his shoes on his hands, / And sang to the goats in the sugarcane lands. / He rode on a bullock cart, facing the back, / And laughed till his glasses went click-clack! What is the rhyme scheme, and what makes the poem funny?
steps: hands/lands rhyme → aa; back/clack rhyme → bb
Funny actions: shoes on hands, singing to goats, riding facing backwards
example.answer: The rhyme scheme is aabb; the silly, upside-down actions of Uncle Bholu make it funny.

learn.reallife: Funny rhymes are used in ads, birthday cards and school function skits because they are easy to remember.

games.title: Poem talk
items: Rhythm is the beat of a poem.
You can clap along to a poem's rhythm.
A couplet is a group of four lines.
A couplet is two lines; four lines is a quatrain.
A humorous poem is meant to make us laugh.
In the rhyme scheme aabb, the first and third lines rhyme.
In aabb, lines 1 and 2 rhyme, and lines 3 and 4 rhyme.

quiz.q: 'Uncle Bholu wore his shoes on his hands.' Why is this line funny?
options: Shoes belong on feet, so it is a silly, upside-down action
quiz.explain: Wearing shoes on hands is the opposite of what we expect — that surprise is funny.
quiz.mistake: Looks for a sensible reason instead of noticing the silliness

quiz.q: 'Uncle Bholu wore his shoes on his hands, / And sang to the goats in the sugarcane lands.' Which word rhymes with 'hands'?
quiz.explain: 'Hands' and 'lands' end with the same '-ands' sound.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a word from the poem that does not rhyme

quiz.q: Two lines next to each other that rhyme are called a:
quiz.explain: A couplet is a pair of rhyming lines.
quiz.mistake: Confuses poetic terms

quiz.q: 'He laughed till his glasses went click-clack!' The words 'click-clack' are an example of:
quiz.explain: 'Click-clack' imitates the sound itself — that is onomatopoeia.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise sound words

quiz.q: What is rhythm in a poem?
options: the beat or pattern of sounds
quiz.explain: Rhythm is the beat you feel when you read a poem aloud.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rhythm with other parts of a poem

quiz.q: The four lines of a poem end with: sun, bed, fun, red. What is the rhyme scheme?
quiz.explain: sun/fun rhyme (a), bed/red rhyme (b), and they alternate: a b a b.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all funny poems are in couplets

quiz.q: A 'humorous' poem is one that is:
quiz.explain: Humorous comes from 'humour', which means fun and laughter.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the word humour

quiz.q: 'He rode on a bullock cart, facing the back.' What does 'facing the back' mean?
options: looking towards the rear instead of the front
quiz.explain: He sat turned around, looking where the cart had been — which is funny.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'back' as a body part

teach.ask: Gappu thinks all poems must be serious. What can make a poem funny?
teach.praise: Ha ha! I'm writing a silly rhyme about a crow in a bow tie!
teach.nudge: What about the actions and the rhymes in a funny poem?

learn.hook: Malayalam is the name of a language — and it reads the same backwards!
points: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: sea/see, flour/flower, knight/night.
Alliteration repeats the same first sound in nearby words: 'Pinky's pet parrot picked papayas.'
Tongue twisters use alliteration to make saying them tricky and fun.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards: madam, level, noon, Malayalam.
A pun is a joke that plays on two meanings of a word or on words that sound alike.

example.q: Explain the joke: 'Why did the bicycle fall over? Because it was two-tired!'
steps: 'Two-tired' means having two tyres.
It sounds just like 'too tired' (very tired).
The joke plays on the two meanings.
example.answer: It is a pun: 'two-tired' (two tyres) sounds like 'too tired'.

learn.reallife: Riddles in children's magazines, jokes on wrappers and ads on hoardings are full of puns and alliteration.

quiz.q: Which pair are homophones?
quiz.explain: Flour and flower sound the same but are spelt differently and mean different things.
quiz.mistake: Confuses homophones with synonyms or antonyms

quiz.q: 'Mr Mehta made many mango milkshakes.' This sentence shows:
quiz.explain: Many words start with the same 'm' sound — that is alliteration.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the repeated first sound

quiz.q: Which word is a palindrome?
quiz.explain: L-E-V-E-L reads the same from both ends.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that only begins and ends with the same letter

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'We bought a kilo of ___ to make rotis.'
quiz.explain: Flour is the powder made from grain; a flower grows on a plant.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the homophones flour and flower

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'The knight rode through the dark ___.'
quiz.explain: 'Night' means the dark time; 'knight' is a soldier on horseback.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the homophones night and knight

quiz.q: 'Why did the bicycle fall over? Because it was two-tired!' The word 'two-tired' sounds like:
quiz.explain: The pun works because 'two-tired' (two tyres) sounds like 'too tired'.
quiz.mistake: Does not hear the sound-alike words in the joke

quiz.q: Which Indian language's name is a palindrome?
quiz.explain: M-A-L-A-Y-A-L-A-M reads the same backwards.
quiz.mistake: Does not check the word letter by letter

quiz.q: Which word is a homophone of 'week'?
quiz.explain: Week (seven days) and weak (not strong) sound the same.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that looks similar but sounds different

teach.ask: Gappu found 'see' and 'sea' and got confused! Explain homophones to him.
teach.praise: I see! I can see the sea! Homophones are fun!
teach.nudge: Do homophones have the same spelling and meaning, or different?

learn.hook: A play is a story that comes alive — actors become the characters right in front of you!
points: 'Say the Right Thing' is a funny play about manners and choosing our words. Here is our own short scene.
A play is a story written to be acted on stage; it is told mostly through dialogue (what the characters say).
The speaker's name comes before each line, and the cast is the list of characters.
Stage directions, usually in brackets or italics, tell actors how to move or speak. They are not spoken aloud.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes. The people who watch are the audience.

example.q: Read: (A busy kitchen. AMMA is rolling rotis. TINU runs in.) TINU: Amma, give me water! AMMA: (raising an eyebrow) Is that how we ask? TINU: (smiling) Amma, may I please have some water? AMMA: Of course, beta. (She hands him a glass.) Which parts are stage directions, and how is Tinu's second line different from his first?
steps: Words in brackets, like '(raising an eyebrow)', are stage directions.
First line: an order — 'give me water!'
Second line: a polite request with 'may I' and 'please'.
example.answer: The bracketed parts are stage directions; Tinu's second line is polite because he uses 'May I please…'.

learn.reallife: School annual-day plays, Ramlila performances and street plays (nukkad natak) all use dialogue and stage directions.

games.title: Play facts
items: Stage directions are read aloud by the actors.
They guide the actors and are not spoken.
A play is told mostly through dialogue.
Characters tell the story by speaking.
A play can be divided into acts and scenes.
Acts are big parts; scenes are smaller parts.
The audience is the group of people who watch a play.
They watch and enjoy the performance.
The cast is the list of characters in a play.
It is usually given at the beginning.

quiz.q: In a play, words in brackets like '(raising an eyebrow)' are called:
quiz.explain: They tell the actor what to do — they are stage directions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks everything in a play is dialogue

quiz.q: Do actors speak the stage directions aloud?
options: Yes, but only at the end
Only the audience reads them aloud
No, stage directions only guide the actors
quiz.explain: Stage directions are instructions for actions and tone; they are not spoken.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every written word in a play is spoken

quiz.q: 'TINU: Amma, give me water!' 'AMMA: Is that how we ask?' Why does Amma say this?
quiz.explain: 'Give me water!' sounds like an order; Amma reminds him to ask nicely.
quiz.mistake: Misses the hint in Amma's question

quiz.q: The conversation between characters in a play is called:
quiz.explain: Dialogue is the talk between characters.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up words from poems and books

quiz.q: The list of all the characters in a play is called the:
quiz.explain: The cast lists the characters (and sometimes the actors who play them).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the cast with the people watching or the place

quiz.q: Plays are usually divided into:
quiz.explain: Acts are the big sections of a play; scenes are smaller parts inside them.
quiz.mistake: Uses the parts of a poem or book

quiz.q: 'TINU: (smiling) Amma, may I please have some water?' Which polite words does Tinu use?
quiz.explain: He asks with 'may I' and adds 'please' — a polite request.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the actual words in the line

quiz.q: The people who watch a play are called the:
quiz.explain: The audience watches; the cast acts; the director guides the actors.
quiz.mistake: Confuses people who watch with people who perform

teach.ask: Gappu wants to act in the school play. How is a play written differently from a story?
teach.praise: Yay! I'll read my lines and follow the stage directions in brackets!
teach.nudge: What do the words in brackets tell the actors?

learn.hook: The same request can sound like a command or a kind question — it all depends on the words you choose!
points: Please, thank you, sorry and excuse me are polite words that make conversations kind.
Polite requests often begin with 'Could you…?', 'Would you…?' or 'May I…?'
'May I' asks for permission. 'Can' usually shows ability: 'Rani can swim.'
When someone thanks you, reply 'You're welcome.'
Our tone of voice and body language also show respect.

example.q: Make this polite: 'Give me your pencil.'
steps: Begin with a polite modal: 'Could you…'
Add 'please'.
Use a gentle verb like 'lend'.
example.answer: Could you please lend me your pencil?

learn.reallife: At home, in shops, on the bus and in class, polite words make people happy to help you.

items.text: ___ I use your phone, please?

quiz.explain: 'Could you please…' is a gentle, polite request.
quiz.mistake: Thinks short commands are fine at the table

quiz.q: If you bump into someone by mistake, you should say:
quiz.explain: We say sorry when we have hurt or troubled someone, even by mistake.

quiz.q: How should you ask to enter the staff room?

quiz.q: Which phrase do we use to get someone's attention politely?

quiz.q: In 'May I go out, sir?', the word 'may' shows:
quiz.explain: Here 'may' is used to ask permission.

quiz.q: In 'Rani can swim very well', the word 'can' shows:
quiz.explain: 'Can' here tells us what Rani is able to do.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'can' always asks for permission

quiz.q: Which sentence is a polite request?

quiz.explain: 'Would you… please?' turns an order into a polite request.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a command with a request

teach.ask: Gappu shouted 'Give me grains!' at the farmer. How should he say it politely?

teach.nudge: Which magic word did you forget? And how can Gappu begin the request?

learn.hook: If your teacher says 'Hold your horses!', don't look for horses in the classroom!
points: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words.
'It's raining cats and dogs' means it is raining heavily — no animals fall from the sky!
Taking an idiom literally (word for word) can cause funny misunderstandings — a common source of humour in plays.
Good communication means choosing words that the listener will understand.
Tone matters: the same words can sound kind or rude depending on how we say them.

example.q: Dadi says, 'Hold your horses!' and Chintu looks around for horses. Why is this funny, and what did Dadi mean?
steps: Chintu takes the words literally.
'Hold your horses' is an idiom.
It means 'wait' or 'be patient'.
example.answer: It's funny because Chintu takes the idiom literally; Dadi meant 'Wait, be patient.'

learn.reallife: Cricket commentators, film dialogues and grandparents all love idioms — knowing them helps you understand people better.

games.title: Idiom meanings
pairs: cost an arm and a leg

quiz.explain: 'The quiz was a piece of cake' means it was very easy.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: What does 'break the ice' mean?
options: start a friendly conversation when people feel shy

quiz.mistake: Reads the words literally

quiz.q: What does 'once in a blue moon' mean?
quiz.explain: Something that happens once in a blue moon happens hardly ever.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is about the real moon

quiz.q: What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
quiz.explain: It means to reveal a secret, often by accident.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: What does 'hold your horses' mean?
quiz.explain: It asks someone to slow down and wait.

quiz.q: What does 'under the weather' mean?

quiz.q: What does 'over the moon' mean?

teach.nudge: Does an idiom mean exactly what its words say?

learn.hook: Every gadget you use — from a pencil sharpener to a mobile phone — began as someone's 'crazy' idea!
points: 'My Brother's Great Invention' is a lesson about a sibling who keeps creating things. Here is our own story on the theme.
To invent is to make something new that did not exist before.
To discover is to find something that already existed but was not known: C. V. Raman discovered the Raman effect in 1928.
Inventors are curious, creative and patient; each failure shows them how to improve.
Word family: invent (verb), invention (noun), inventor (person), inventive (adjective).

example.q: Read: My brother Kunal tied an old umbrella, two spoons and a toy motor together. "Behold the Mango-Picker 3000!" he announced. The machine wobbled, buzzed and shook the branch — and one ripe mango dropped straight onto his head. Kunal rubbed his head and grinned. "Version two will have a basket," he said. What does 'Version two will have a basket' show about Kunal?
steps: The machine shook the mango loose, but it fell on his head — a small failure.
Kunal grins instead of getting upset.
He already plans an improvement: a basket to catch the mango.
example.answer: He learns from his mistake and plans to improve his invention — he is creative and does not give up.

learn.reallife: India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February, the day in 1928 when C. V. Raman announced his discovery.

teach.nudge: Which word is for making something new, and which is for finding something that already exists?

learn.hook: One tiny mark — the apostrophe — tells you whether the robot belongs to one brother or to three!
points: Siblings are brothers and sisters. Friendly competition between them is called sibling rivalry.
To show that something belongs to one person, add 's: my brother's invention.
For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: my brothers' room (two or more brothers).
For a plural noun not ending in s, add 's: the children's toys, the women's team.
Its = belonging to it (The cat licked its paw). It's = it is (It's raining).

example.q: I have one sister. Is it 'my sisters' bicycle' or 'my sister's bicycle'?
steps: Only one sister owns the bicycle → singular noun.
For a singular noun we add 's.
example.answer: my sister's bicycle

learn.reallife: Name boards like 'Sharma's Sweets' or 'Children's Park' use apostrophes to show who something belongs to.

quiz.explain: 'Sisters' is a plural ending in s, so add only an apostrophe: sisters'.

learn.hook: Even a great inventor needs clear steps — or the machine ends up upside down!
points: Instructions tell how to make or do something, step by step.
They use imperative sentences — commands or requests that usually begin with a verb: 'Cut the paper.' The subject 'you' is understood.
Sequence words show order: first, next, then, after that, finally.
A list of materials (things needed) comes before the steps.
Other kinds of sentences: assertive (statement), interrogative (question) and exclamatory (strong feeling).

example.q: Write instructions for making nimbu pani (lemonade).
steps: Materials: a glass of water, one lemon, sugar, a pinch of salt.
First, squeeze the lemon into the water.
Next, add sugar and a pinch of salt.
Then stir well.
Finally, serve it cool.
example.answer: First squeeze the lemon, next add sugar and salt, then stir, and finally serve.

learn.reallife: Recipe books, game rules, medicine labels and model kits all use imperative sentences and sequence words.

quiz.explain: It gives a command and begins with the verb 'fold'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence about a task is imperative

quiz.q: In 'Stir the mixture well', who is the understood subject?
quiz.explain: Imperative sentences speak to the listener, so 'you' is understood.
quiz.mistake: Thinks imperatives have no subject at all

quiz.q: Which word best begins the last step of instructions?
quiz.explain: 'Finally' signals the last step.

quiz.q: 'Please shut the door.' What kind of sentence is this?
quiz.explain: It is a polite request or command, so it is imperative.

quiz.q: 'What a clever invention!' What kind of sentence is this?

quiz.q: 'Did your brother build this?' What kind of sentence is this?
quiz.explain: It asks a question and ends with a question mark.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to tell his friend how to build a nest. How should he write the instructions?
teach.praise: First, collect twigs. Next, weave them... I can write instructions now!
teach.nudge: What kind of word should each step begin with, and how do we show the order?

learn.hook: Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthems of TWO countries — India's and Bangladesh's!
points: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was a poet, writer, musician and painter from Bengal, lovingly called Gurudev.
In 1913 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature — the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize.
He wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', India's national anthem.
He started a school at Santiniketan in West Bengal, which grew into Visva-Bharati University.
His poem 'Paper Boats' shows a child sending boats down a stream, dreaming they will reach faraway lands. Below is our own poem on that idea.

example.q: Read: I fold my homework sheet into a boat, / And set it on the stream where raindrops float. / I draw a smiling sun in crayon blue — / Dear stranger, will this boat sail all the way to you? What does the child hope for?
steps: The child sets the boat on a stream.
The child draws a smiling sun on it.
'Dear stranger' — the child hopes someone far away will find it.
example.answer: The child hopes the boat will travel far and reach a stranger in another place.

learn.reallife: Every time you sing 'Jana Gana Mana' in the school assembly, you are singing Tagore's words.

learn.hook: 'My dreams are kites' — can a dream really be a kite? In a poem, it can!
points: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as': 'The boat bobbed like a duck.'
A metaphor says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The stream was a silver ribbon.'
Similes and metaphors paint pictures in the reader's mind.
Common similes: as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, as cool as a cucumber, as light as a feather.
We use 'will' to talk about future dreams: 'One day I will become a pilot.'

example.q: Simile or metaphor? (a) 'The paper boat floated like a leaf.' (b) 'Childhood is a garden of dreams.'
steps: (a) uses 'like' → simile
(b) says childhood IS a garden, no 'like' or 'as' → metaphor
example.answer: (a) is a simile; (b) is a metaphor.

learn.reallife: Film songs, poems and even everyday talk ('She's a star!') are full of similes and metaphors.

learn.hook: Before phones, travellers wrote letters — and a single letter could carry a whole journey inside it!
points: 'North, South, East, West' is a lesson made of letters written from different parts of India. Here we learn to write such letters.
An informal letter is written to family or friends in a warm, chatty style.
Parts of an informal letter: sender's address, date, salutation (Dear Anu,), body, closing (With love,) and name.
A formal letter (to a principal or an officer) uses 'Sir/Madam', a subject line and a closing like 'Yours sincerely'.
Travel letters describe places, food, weather, people and feelings. P.S. (postscript) adds a note after the letter ends.

example.q: Read: Dear Anu, Greetings from Shillong! It rained three times today, and the hills wore a cap of clouds. We ate hot momos near the market. I wish you were here! With love, Tara. P.S. I'm bringing you a pineapple! Find the salutation, the closing and the postscript.
steps: 'Dear Anu,' greets the reader → salutation.
'With love, Tara' ends the letter → closing and name.
'P.S. I'm bringing you a pineapple!' is added at the end → postscript.
example.answer: Salutation: 'Dear Anu,' — Closing: 'With love, Tara' — Postscript: 'P.S. I'm bringing you a pineapple!'

learn.reallife: Emails and holiday messages follow the same idea: greet, share your news, close warmly.

teach.nudge: How does a letter begin, and how does it end?

learn.hook: Travel from Ladakh to Kanyakumari and you'll pass snow, deserts, rainforests and beaches — all in one country!

East and North-east: West Bengal, Odisha and Assam; Bihu is celebrated in Assam. West: Gujarat and Rajasthan; the Thar Desert lies mostly in Rajasthan.
Culture means a group's way of life — food, language, clothes, festivals, music and dance.

learn.hook: Over the bridge, through the tunnel, along the river — tiny words guide every journey!
points: A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun is related to another word, often by place, direction or time.
Place: in, on, under, between, beside, near, behind, at.
Direction or movement: to, towards, into, across, along, through, up, down.
'In' shows position inside; 'into' shows movement from outside to inside.
'Between' is used for two people or things; 'among' for more than two.

example.q: Fill the blanks: 'The ferry went ___ the river, and we walked ___ the bank to the temple.'
steps: Going from one side to the other side → across
Moving beside the length of the bank → along
example.answer: across, along

learn.reallife: Maps, signboards and GPS directions use prepositions: 'Turn left at the signal, go across the bridge.'

In 'The cat is under the bed', 'under' is a preposition.

learn.hook: What's waiting at the other end of a dark tunnel? Adventure stories keep you guessing!
points: 'The Tunnel' is an adventure story set around a railway tunnel in a forest. Here is our own short adventure.
An adventure story has excitement, a challenge or danger, and a character who shows courage.
Story elements: setting, characters, problem (conflict), climax (most exciting point) and resolution (how it ends).
Writers build suspense with short sentences, sound words and unanswered questions.
Courage does not mean feeling no fear — it means facing your fear.

example.q: Read: The moment the train entered the tunnel, the whole compartment went black. Ishaan gripped the window bar. The wheels roared, and his heart drummed fast. He counted slowly — one, two, three… At twenty, a burst of green and gold light flooded in: paddy fields and a sparkling river. "That wasn't scary at all," he grinned. What is the problem, the climax and the resolution?
steps: Problem: the dark tunnel makes Ishaan scared.
Climax: the roaring darkness while he counts.
Resolution: light floods in and he smiles — his fear is gone.
example.answer: Problem — fear of the dark tunnel; climax — the roaring dark while he counts; resolution — the bright fields appear and he grins.

learn.reallife: Train journeys through the Western Ghats pass through many tunnels — a real-life mini adventure!

games.title: Story elements
items: The climax is the most exciting point of a story.
It is the high point of tension.
The resolution comes at the very beginning of a story.
The resolution comes at the end, when the problem is solved.
Short sentences can help build suspense.
They make the reader read faster and feel tense.
The setting tells us where and when a story takes place.
Here the setting is a train in a tunnel.
A brave person never feels any fear.
Brave people may feel afraid but still face the challenge.

learn.hook: India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 — and today Indian Railways carries crores of people!
points: Railway words: platform, compartment (coach), engine (locomotive), track, signal, guard, tunnel.

Safety first: stand behind the yellow line on the platform and cross only by the footbridge.

learn.hook: 'I was waiting when the train came.' — two past tenses in one sentence, working as a team!
points: Simple past tells about a finished action: The train arrived at six.
Past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) tells about an action in progress in the past: I was waiting.
Together: 'While we were waiting, the train arrived.' The longer action is past continuous; the short one that interrupts is simple past.
Use 'was' with I, he, she, it and singular nouns; 'were' with you, we, they and plural nouns.
Watch irregular verbs: run → ran, catch → caught, ring → rang; and spelling: stop → stopped.

example.q: Fix this sentence: 'I was eat my lunch when the train come.'
steps: The longer action is in progress → was + eating
The short action interrupts → simple past 'came'
example.answer: I was eating my lunch when the train came.

learn.reallife: When you tell a friend what happened on a trip, you naturally use both tenses: 'We were singing when the bus stopped!'

topics.title: A poem of longing to travel

learn.hook: Have you ever heard a train at night and wondered where it was going?
points: 'Travel' is a poem in which the speaker hears trains and longs to go on a journey. Here is our own poem on that feeling.
Longing means a strong wish for something you do not have.
The speaker is the voice in the poem (the 'I'); it may or may not be the poet.
Mood is the feeling a poem creates — here it is dreamy and restless.
Poets use personification ('a whistle calls my name') and similes ('like flame') to show feelings.

example.q: Read: Each night a far-off whistle calls my name, / The lights of passing trains go by like flame. / My books stay open, but my thoughts have flown / To mountain roads and towns I've never known. How does the speaker feel, and which words show it?
steps: 'calls my name' — the speaker feels the journey is calling.
'my thoughts have flown' — the mind is already far away.
'towns I've never known' — a wish to see new places.
example.answer: The speaker feels a restless longing to travel; 'calls my name', 'thoughts have flown' and 'towns I've never known' show it.

learn.reallife: Looking at a map, a travel show or an aeroplane in the sky and wishing you were going somewhere — that's longing!

games.title: Mood words

games.title: Poem check
items: Longing is a strong wish for something.
The speaker of a poem is always the poet's best friend.
The speaker is the voice in the poem.
'A whistle calls my name' is an example of personification.
A whistle cannot really call a name.
'Go by like flame' is a simile.
The mood of a poem is the number of lines in it.
Mood is the feeling the poem creates.

quiz.q: What does 'longing' mean?
quiz.explain: Longing is a deep wish, such as a wish to travel.

quiz.explain: The books are open, but the mind has wandered off to travel.

quiz.q: What is the mood of the poem about the far-off whistle?
quiz.explain: The speaker is dreaming of roads and towns and cannot settle down to study.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the feeling behind the words

quiz.explain: The speaker is the 'I' in the poem.

learn.hook: Close your eyes: 'hot, crispy pakoras on a rainy evening'. Can you smell them? That's imagery!
points: Imagery is language that helps us see, hear, smell, taste or feel something in our minds.
Sight imagery: 'golden mustard fields'. Sound imagery: 'the engine roared'.
Smell imagery: 'the scent of wet earth'. Taste: 'tangy chaat'. Touch: 'the cold window glass'.
Strong imagery uses exact nouns, vivid adjectives and strong verbs.
Compare: 'The train went.' with 'The train thundered over the iron bridge.'

example.q: Make this sentence vivid: 'The bus went up the hill.'
steps: Add a colour or detail: red bus
Choose a strong verb: rattled
Add a setting detail: misty hill
example.answer: The red bus rattled up the misty hill.

learn.reallife: Travel posters, food ads and good storybooks use imagery to make you want to go, taste or read more.

learn.hook: At the top of Mount Everest, the air has only about one-third as much oxygen as at sea level!
points: 'Conquering the Summit' is about mountaineering and the grit it takes to reach the top.
Mount Everest (8,849 m) is the highest mountain in the world. It lies on the border of Nepal and China (Tibet).
Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary were the first to reach its summit, on 29 May 1953.
Bachendri Pal became the first Indian woman to climb Everest, in 1984.
Mountaineering words: summit, base camp, expedition, altitude, ice axe, crampons, oxygen cylinder.

example.q: Why do climbers on very high mountains carry oxygen cylinders?
steps: Altitude means height above sea level.
The higher you go, the thinner the air, so there is less oxygen in each breath.
Extra oxygen helps climbers breathe and stay safe.
example.answer: Because the air at great heights has much less oxygen, so they carry extra oxygen to breathe safely.

learn.reallife: Mountaineering institutes in Darjeeling, Uttarkashi and Manali train young climbers in safety and teamwork.

learn.hook: Add '-ation' to 'determine' and you get the one word every mountaineer needs: determination!
points: Determination is a strong will to reach your goal, even when it is hard.
Suffixes are added at the end of a word and can change its class: determine → determination, achieve → achievement.
-ous, -ful and -less make adjectives: courage → courageous, hope → hopeful, fear → fearless. (-ful = full of; -less = without)
-ly makes many adverbs: brave → bravely, tireless → tirelessly.
A character's actions show their qualities: trying again every day shows determination.

example.q: Read: When Pema first tried to climb the hill behind her school in Sikkim, she stopped halfway, out of breath. The next morning, she tried again. Every day she climbed a little higher, carrying her water bottle and a smile. By winter, she reached the top without stopping and saw the snowy peaks glowing in the sun. Which quality does Pema show, and which words prove it?
steps: She stopped halfway at first.
'The next morning, she tried again.' and 'Every day she climbed a little higher.'
She did not give up until she reached the top.
example.answer: Determination — she tried again every day until she reached the top.

learn.reallife: Athletes, students preparing for exams and farmers waiting for the monsoon all need determination.

quiz.explain: The suffix -ation turns the verb 'determine' into the noun 'determination'.

learn.hook: 'She has climbed Everest!' — the present perfect connects a past action to right now.
points: Present perfect = has/have + past participle: She has climbed. They have reached.
Use 'has' with he, she, it and singular nouns; 'have' with I, you, we, they and plural nouns.
It is used for actions finished at an unstated time or with a result now; words like just, already, yet, ever, never go with it.
Do not use it with a definite past time (yesterday, in 1953) — use simple past: 'Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953.'
'Since' + a point of time (since 2019); 'for' + a length of time (for six months).

example.q: Choose correctly: 'Riya (has reached / reached) base camp yesterday.'
steps: 'Yesterday' is a definite past time.
The present perfect is not used with a definite past time.
So we use simple past.
example.answer: Riya reached base camp yesterday.

learn.reallife: News headlines often use the present perfect: 'Indian team has won the gold!'

games.title: Present perfect rules
items: 'Has' is used with he, she and it.

The present perfect uses has/have + past participle.

'I have climbed the hill yesterday' is correct.
With 'yesterday' we use simple past: 'I climbed the hill yesterday.'
'Since' is used with a point of time, like 'since Monday'.
'For' is used with a length of time.
'Went' is the simple past; the past participle is 'gone'.

quiz.explain: Three months is a length of time, so we use 'for'.

chapters.title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers

learn.hook: Whether it is snowy mountains, deep seas or the open sky, someone is keeping watch over India every minute.
points: 'A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers' honours the men and women who protect our country. Homage means deep respect shown to honour someone.
India's armed forces are the Army (land), the Navy (sea) and the Air Force (air).
The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.
Army Day is on 15 January, Air Force Day on 8 October and Navy Day on 4 December.
Soldiers also help people during floods, earthquakes and other disasters with rescue and relief.

example.q: A flood hits a village. Which forces might help, and how?
steps: The Army can rescue people and set up relief camps.
The Navy can send boats and divers.
The Air Force can fly helicopters to drop food and lift people to safety.
example.answer: All three can help: the Army on land, the Navy with boats and divers, and the Air Force with helicopters.

learn.reallife: On Republic Day, the parade on Kartavya Path in New Delhi shows marching contingents of the Army, Navy and Air Force.

learn.hook: 'Param Vir' means 'the bravest of the brave' — the name of India's highest wartime gallantry award.
points: Patriotism means love for one's country; a patriot is a person who loves and serves the country.
Sacrifice means giving up something precious for the sake of others.
Gallantry and valour both mean great bravery. Valiant means very brave; its opposite is cowardly.
The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest wartime gallantry award; the Ashoka Chakra is the highest peacetime gallantry award.
The National War Memorial in New Delhi honours soldiers who gave their lives for the nation.

example.q: Why do people stand in silence at a war memorial?
steps: A memorial reminds us of soldiers who gave their lives.
Silence is a way of showing deep respect.
It helps us remember their sacrifice.
example.answer: To show respect and remember the soldiers' sacrifice for the nation.

learn.reallife: Many schools collect money on Armed Forces Flag Day (7 December) for the welfare of soldiers and their families.

quiz.explain: Patriotism is love and loyalty for one's country.

quiz.explain: The Param Vir Chakra is the highest wartime gallantry award. Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian award; the Arjuna Award is for sports.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up gallantry awards with civilian or sports awards

quiz.q: What is India's highest peacetime gallantry award?
quiz.explain: The Ashoka Chakra is the highest gallantry award for bravery away from the battlefield.

quiz.explain: The National War Memorial is in New Delhi, near India Gate.

quiz.explain: Soldiers sacrifice comfort, time with family and sometimes their lives.

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'brave'?
quiz.explain: Valiant means brave. The others mean fearful.
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'brave'?
quiz.explain: Cowardly means lacking courage — the opposite of brave.
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

teach.ask: Gappu saw people standing silently at a war memorial. Why do they do that? Explain sacrifice and patriotism.
teach.praise: I'll bow my little head too. Thank you, brave soldiers.
teach.nudge: What did the soldiers give for the country, and how do we honour them?

learn.hook: 'The soldier saved the child' or 'The child was saved by the soldier' — same event, different focus!
points: In the active voice, the subject does the action: The soldiers built the bridge.
In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: The bridge was built by the soldiers.
Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle (+ by the doer).
Simple present passive: is/are + past participle. Simple past passive: was/were + past participle.
We use the passive when the doer is unknown or less important: The fort was built long ago.

example.q: Change to passive: 'The Navy rescued the fishermen.'
steps: Object 'the fishermen' becomes the subject.
Past tense, plural subject → were + past participle 'rescued'.
Add 'by the Navy'.
example.answer: The fishermen were rescued by the Navy.

learn.reallife: News reports often use the passive: 'Hundreds of people were rescued from the floods.'

games.title: Active or passive?
items: A bridge was built by the soldiers.
The flag was hoisted by the captain.
The plane was flown by the pilot.
The villagers are helped by the army.

quiz.q: Change to passive: 'The soldiers built the bridge.'
options: The soldiers were built by the bridge.
The bridge was built by the soldiers.
The bridge is building by the soldiers.
quiz.explain: The object becomes the subject; past tense → was + built; add 'by the soldiers'.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the words without changing the verb correctly

quiz.q: Change to passive: 'The army helps the villagers.'
options: The villagers is helped by the army.
The army is helped by the villagers.
The villagers are helped by the army.
The villagers were helped by the army.
quiz.explain: Simple present with a plural subject → are + helped.
quiz.mistake: Changes the tense while changing the voice

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: The captain is hoisting the flag.
The flag was hoisted by the captain.
The captain will hoist the flag.
quiz.explain: The subject (the flag) receives the action, and the verb is was + hoisted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any past tense sentence is passive

quiz.q: Change to active: 'The medal was given by the President.'
options: The President was given the medal.
quiz.explain: The doer (the President) becomes the subject; 'was given' becomes 'gave'.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the passive verb or changes the tense

quiz.q: 'The parade ___ watched by thousands of people.'
quiz.explain: 'Parade' is singular, so we use 'was' + watched.
quiz.mistake: Matches the verb to 'people' instead of the subject 'parade'

quiz.q: 'The letters were ___ by the soldiers.'
quiz.explain: The passive needs the past participle: write – wrote – written.
quiz.mistake: Uses the simple past instead of the past participle

quiz.q: 'The rescue boats ___ sent by the Navy.'
quiz.explain: 'Boats' is plural and the action is in the past, so 'were' is correct.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'was' with a plural subject

quiz.q: Why is the passive used in 'The fort was built long ago'?
options: The doer is unknown or not important
quiz.explain: We don't know or need to say who built the fort, so the passive fits.
quiz.mistake: Does not know when the passive is useful

teach.ask: Gappu read 'The village was saved by the soldiers' and asked who did the action. Explain active and passive voice.
teach.praise: So the soldiers did the saving! Passive puts the village first. Clever!
teach.nudge: Which voice puts the doer first, and which puts the receiver first?

learn.hook: The Siachen Glacier is called the world's highest battlefield — soldiers guard it in freezing cold!
points: 'My Dear Soldiers' is a poem that thanks and honours our soldiers. Here is our own tribute poem.
A tribute is something said, written or done to show respect and thanks.
Poets use contrast to show how tough a soldier's job is: icy Siachen and the hot Thar Desert.
The Siachen Glacier in Ladakh is known as the highest battlefield in the world.
The tone of such poems is grateful, proud and respectful.

example.q: Read: On Siachen's ice where the cold winds blow, / In Thar's hot sands where few dare go, / On stormy seas and skies so high, / You stand on guard as days roll by. / We sleep in peace, we laugh, we play — / Dear soldiers, thank you, every day. What contrast does the poet show, and what is the tone?
steps: Cold 'Siachen's ice' is set against 'Thar's hot sands'.
Soldiers guard land, sea and sky.
'Dear soldiers, thank you' shows gratitude.
example.answer: The poet contrasts freezing ice with hot sand to show soldiers guard everywhere; the tone is grateful and respectful.

learn.reallife: Students across India send rakhis, cards and letters to soldiers posted at the borders to say thank you.

games.title: About the poem

The Thar Desert is covered with ice.
The Thar is a hot, sandy desert.
